utterances.text: At the time, you told us what position you occupied and as far as I understand it you did nonetheless have some kind of direct contact with the political leadership of Croatia, did you not, at least in the sense of receiving information, which they gave you ex officio. Do you happen to know that at that time, it was the position of the political Croatian leadership that they should not allow the civilian population to leave their territory, specifically to leave the territory of Vukovar, because this could be taken to be ethnic cleansing? In the political echelons of power in Croatia, were there any ideas along those lines?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the demands were that the population should not move out from certain areas. However, not because this would imply ethnic cleansing of any kind but because of their support to the defenders. And following on from military logic, if the weaker side defends itself and the civilians have completely left a certain area and territory, then the defence is far less effective and far weaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask several questions of you which have to do with your answers yesterday about the October evacuation. All of us here in the courtroom are interested in those events. Yesterday I understood that, according to you, in October there was one convoy which came to the barracks, couldn't get to the hospital, was sent back and then returned several days later and then the evacuation was carried out. This is how I understood your testimony about that evacuation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was. That was the first convoy that was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were now to give you my information, which is that this first convoy organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres arrived indeed on the 14th of October to the barracks in Vukovar, and when it was supposed to continue on to the hospital, the defenders or, rather, Borkovic and his men, did not allow them to pass through the territory which they held between the barracks and the hospital. Their military position was that the JNA would follow the convoy, and that that was in fact the reason the convoy was sent back. A completely different convoy with different vehicles arrived four days later, once again organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres, and they did reach the hospital. Does that refresh your recollection of it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that Borkovic reacted in that way and it is likely that he did. Quite likely, because such a development of events and such a logic were reasonable. Whether different vehicles arrived four days later, I don't know. But I don't think that that was the case, because this organisation, Medecins Sans Frontieres, who were the organisers, who were the sponsors, and those responsible for the convoys, barely managed to get together the vehicles that were used the first time. So in my view, it wasn't very likely that they were able to obtain a different set of vehicles. However, if you know better, I'm not going to deny this. I don't know all of the details. I know that there were many complications, stop, go, and so on. I mentioned yesterday Lieutenant Colonel Milenkovic, who inspected the convoy and then the nurse was taken off the convoy because there were some suspicions regarding her. I know that there were a lot of complications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: You were a security organ, and if there is a suspicion that somebody was entering the territory under your control and wanted to take advantage of that in order to transport a person that should not be transported or supplies that should not be transported, what is the job of the security organ? Should the security organ conduct an inspection?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be done either by a security organ or by the police. At any rate everybody protects themselves and wants to know who is entering the territory they control. However, if we are talking about Medecins Sans Frontieres, if we are talking about the European monitors, then these are the organisations which should verify that the purpose of the convoy is strictly observed, that it is used only for those limited purposes, not for transporting arms and the -- such organisations as Medecins Sans Frontieres and the Red Cross should take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. A soldier of JNA was supposed to be transported in that convoy against his will to Zagreb. He gave some information to somebody in the Vukovar Hospital and once the convoy was inspected, he was found and he was taken off the convoy. Was there perhaps a fear that something like that could be attempted?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that case. Yes, there is a possibility that that happened. Every side has their own scheming, so if they succeed in it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If needed, I will ask that the Exhibit that we discussed be placed in front of you. I think the one we discussed yesterday or the day before, which is the agreement dated the 8th of October 1991 about cease-fire, if I can call it that, and unblocking of barracks. If you want, it can be placed in front of you, but since you were one of the signatories of this agreement I assume that you know very well that it also set forth that the barracks should be unblocked and that the movement of people and goods should be unhindered. This is what it regulated, is it right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also gave evidence about a document, Exhibit 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can place it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this is your document I believe you're quite familiar with it. This is a letter to Mr. Anton Tus dated the 18th of October, 1991, meaning after the period, and the letter was directed to you and to the European mission. It discusses the evacuation, the October evacuation, of the hospital. The second paragraph of that document or, rather, the last passage is something that I'm interested in. It discusses the alleged removal of equipment from the airport in Pula. General Tus says there: Can you please read out the last passage, read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the Pula airport, they are taking out the airport equipment, not owned by the Yugoslav army, and the kidnapped plane of the Uganda airliner, Boeing 707 is used to transport it elsewhere outside of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following passage. Would you please read it out, the next one?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "We kindly ask that you put an end to this and similar action. Otherwise, we shall shoot down such transport planes which we haven't done so far for fear that they might be transporting family members of JNA members leaving the airports in Pula and Zadar."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. This happened after the agreement. What is your position concerning the order of your superior to shoot down the planes transporting the family members of the JNA servicemen leaving airports? It sounds quite ominous to me.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a misinterpretation of what is stated here. What is stated here reads as follows: "Should similar action continue, the removal of equipment and so on" because the JNA had already started withdrawing at that point, "We shall open fire which is something we haven't done so far, for fear that the family members of the JNA servicemen were in the planes." This means we didn't shoot the planes because we didn't want to shoot down the planes carrying the families of JNA servicemen leaving these airports and it was a well known fact that they were leaving the airports. This is how Tus and I interpret this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I misinterpreted it but it is up to the Trial Chamber to evaluate this. Now I would like to turn briefly to Exhibit 101. You spoke about this document as well. This is a letter sent by Iljo Kobas, professor. I'm interested in one or two items from this document. Based on this document, we can't see when it was dispatched. There is only some information given up in the upper portion which I think is when it was faxed. My question is: When did you receive this letter? Do you remember when it arrived?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date here, the 15th of March 1992, at nine in the morning. I can see this in the upper portion after the ERN number. Most likely it was on that day, because this is what the fax machine printed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the letter, it says that according to the information, the JNA had left the village and the Chetniks entered from the village of Cakovci. Do you know where this village Cakovci is located in relation to the village of Boksic?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Cakovci is in Eastern Slavonia, near Vukovar. The village of Boksic is most likely located next to it but I don't know this precisely. I have no reason to distrust the letter of the secretary, Iljo Kobas, because I'm sure he was familiar with the situation because he was a local man. He was in the vicinity of Cakovci. Not in the immediate vicinity but he -- Zupanja was one of the nearby free cities near Vukovar, and it seems that he learned this from the refugees who had arrived in Zupanja and where they found accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it too. Please tell us this: Do you know when the JNA left the village of Boksic or that area? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have that territory under our control at the time. This is three months after the occupation of the eastern part of Slavonia. It seems it is clear that the source of the information was somebody from Boksic, a refugee who came and gave information to Iljo Kobas, the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another interesting place mentioned in the document is Lipovac. Would you agree with me that Lipovac is at the border between Croatia and Serbia or, at the time, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that Lipovac was a place where frequently exchanges were carried out of war prisoners and through which civilians passed. Mr. Grujic participated in it, Amir Masovic, and General Mladenovic [as interpreted]. Are you familiar with these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said General Radinovic. The name Mladenovic is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Serbs who had been deported from Serbia and Bosnia also passed through Lipovac?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lipovac has a fate typical for border towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I will turn to another topic. What was the reason you were replaced from the post of chief in March of 1991? Did you receive an -- official or unofficial information about this?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information, or notice, from my commander of the 5th Corps. He said to me that my chief of the security department of the air force had informed him that I was to turn over the keys to my deputy. At the time I asked the commander to establish the reasons for my removal, telling him that in three months he himself would be replaced unless he objected to my removal. And I was wrong. He was removed after four months, on the 2nd of July. This was Major General Marijan Rozic. I was removed from my post or what triggered it, because the reasons for it were much deeper, was that I opposed the assessment of my superior, General Rakocevic about the reasons for events in Pakrac in March of 1991 and the role of JNA in those events. You probably remember, based on later developments, that I was actually right. My superior at the time stated, and the media carried it, that a large number of Serbs in Pakrac had been arrested, killed, expelled into forests, whereas in fact something quite different had happened. They also said that the JNA protected the Serb population there. I said that that wasn't true. The commission which investigated this and which was headed by Tupurkovski established that that wasn't true. The role of the JNA in the Pakrac events was found to be precisely what I described it to be, which was a setup by the security services. That was the reason why I was removed from office, and I was happy that it happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spent more than five years in that post. Can you tell us specifically or not so specifically, during that period of five years, or perhaps even a longer period, seven to eight years, how many pieces of security information or intelligence information you passed on to your superiors, to your commanders, or those who were your immediate superiors in the professional chain of command, about the activity of Croatian immigration in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not supply a single piece of intelligence information because I was not a member of intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But as a security organ, if you received some information, would you put it in a drawer?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a security organ, I would pass on security information but not intelligence information. In that sense, it was my duty to evaluate the information I received and to collect such information in any way and then include my comment and propose measures and send it to my superior. Simultaneously, if there was any information of interest to the command superiors, to the military organisation, I was to inform the relevant superior about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand all that and that is derived from the rule that we discussed. If you acquired some intelligence information, would you react in any way to that information in relation to anyone?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? Are you thinking about intelligence data or security-related data of interest? If it's an intelligence information, then I would forward it to the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is what I wanted to hear. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence information is dealt with by the intelligence personnel, so this is a separate structure within the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever submit any kind of report to the security organ relating to Croatian nationalist extremists amongst your ranks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you do that from 1990 or 1989 onwards, when the authorities changed, when the changes began?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that happened in my domain, within the 5th Corps, and had any even suggestion of nationalist overtones would be passed along the security service line and would reach my superiors. That would be the usual way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You probably know that in October, on the 12th of October 1990, two trailer trucks of Tazmatrans [phoen] arrived with large quantities of weapons from Hungary. You're probably aware of this. If nothing else you would have learned about it from the media.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it. Not from that date perhaps, but this was something that was discussed a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Pleso airport is a military and civilian airport, that's what it was at the same time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a mixed airport then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that on the 13th of October 1990, an airplane landed from the German Democratic Republic bearing weapons at that airport?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was from the GDR and I don't know whether there were weapons there. I know that an airplane landed, a Kikasev [phoen] plane, but I don't know about what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, before the break, you said that I should ask you about airplanes so this is what I'm doing now?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 21st of November, an airplane landed from Panama bearing an arms delivery? These were 5.000 pieces of Zbrojovka pistols?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 21st of November 1990. Yes, I'm talking about 1990.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that particular instance but I know that a certain quantity of pistols was obtained by organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in that period, around Christmas, New Year, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that weapons arrived on the 28th of November 1990, by plane from Frankfurt?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that but there is the possibility of that. I didn't know that. I didn't have a way of knowing that. I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not a flight controller?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, flight controller would control flights but would not know anything about the cargos?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are customs organs, there is also organs of the MUP that monitor the transport that planes bring in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then there was a Ugandan plane, a Boeing 707, it was mentioned in a document we looked at before. According to my information, on the 13th of January 1991, it made a forced landing. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but it was landed by force by the air force to Pleso airport?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was in January. Perhaps this was sometime in September 1991. Perhaps it was in July, August, or September of that year. It's hard for me to remember but it was not January. I am aware of that incident because this was something that was immediately covered by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you heard about it from the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Kikasev plane is something that I learned about from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you, as a senior JNA officer and still are -- that's what you were at the time -- how did you react to the killing of a JNA soldier in Split, soldier Sasa Gresovski [phoen] at the barracks in Split?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally at that time, and also now, consider that to be a very uncivilised act, a gesture. To prevent somebody in that way in the implementation of his assignment, that person, that young soldier, was assigned duties there, but at the time, passions were so high and this happened. These people were brought to trial, they served their sentence, and they were held responsible for their acts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you a question. I think you either responded to a question by the Prosecutor or to my colleague Vasic about it. It relates to the A, B, and C plans, and these are borders -- options A and B and you also drew some boundaries, Karlovac, Virovitica, Karlobag. I know that these ideas actually stem from the position of certain political parties from Serbia, specifically I'm talking about the positions of Vojislav Seselj. However, I did not see any single military document that would mention this. This is not mentioned in any military documents. Mr. Kadijevic or other people who were very much aware of clear JNA positions in that regard were not aware of that either. Do you know of any documents where this boundary is actually mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to regulations, I didn't actually see that document because of my position. However, all the recollections and the writings of those who participated in the events at the time made it quite realistic to me to make such assessments which I stated at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you react when you say the famous TV footage of Spegelj stating - Spegelj actually at the time was defence minister; isn't that correct, to make it clear to the Trial Chamber - That every JNA officer was covered by five people and each one of them would be cut down at home if necessary. When you saw that footage, how did you react? This was in February 1990; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This actually happened on the 25th of January, 1991, as I recall. I had a general view about that footage and I still hold that view, that this was a setup by the JNA security service, that they used some statements by Spegelj, which he had made in his own company, among his acquaintances, either for psychological effect or for some other purposes, this was used by the service. That was my opinion at the time, and I still maintain that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we will bring people to the courtroom who have direct knowledge about that footage. I put the question to you. You have answered. So I'm satisfied with your answer. Even laymen knew at the time that the Croatian defence ministry transferred a large number of conscripts or transported or moved, shifted, a large number of conscripts to the police reserves. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that now but at the time I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a general question: Who makes the reserve forces' distribution or deployment on behalf of the JNA? Who would replenish units for -- that require that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is done by the secretariat for defence. They make lists of conscripts. They mobilise them, send them to serve their regular military terms, and they also assign them to their combat units once they have completed their term of office -- of service. And they do this on the basis of the requirements of units for certain specialised services or duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are plans then initiated at the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not really informed about that at that level, because my duties were different. So this is not something that I really learned anything about and what methods were used in order to recruit conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps then you don't know the answer to the question, but I will put it any way: Who has the priority when replenishment of units is concerned? Are they military units, police, reserve police or Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the priority goes to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Milosevic case, and I also heard a similar view expressed by you here, you said "the so-called Spegelj affair." Then you said -- this was already in the transcript on page 11, when you testified on the 30th of June 2003, you said the so-called illegal channels used by Spegelj. What I'm interested in is: Why do you use the word "alleged" or "so-called"? Do you believe that everything Spegelj did was legal?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spegelj was the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia, in charge of organising the defence of the Republic of Croatia, and also he was entrusted with assessing, along with other subjects from the political leadership, the danger. He made the estimate that we know he made. The political leadership agreed with it, and then he set out to enable the defence to be able to carry out the defence tasks, to defend the Republic of Croatia. In that sense, weapons were required. He tried to obtain weapons through this federal Secretariat for National Defence. He did not receive the weapons. Barricades were already set up on the territory of Croatia. So what else could he do other than import weapons from abroad? As far as the Croatian authorities were concerned, these were legal tasks and legal channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, as a JNA officer at that time, whether these were legal tasks and legal channels?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as a legal JNA officer, were -- think that these were -- the.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is not sure whether the witness said legal or illegal channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In those terms, did you -- would you please repeat your last answer? It was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, as a JNA officer at the time believed them to be illegal channels at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This information about the illegal channels to procure weapons, was that something you found out through the media or did you find that out through your regular activities in your job?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, as chief of security of the 5th Corps, was not authorised, nor did I have anything to do in relation to civilian authorities. There were -- detachments of counter-intelligence groups were formed for that purpose earlier and I mentioned that, and they worked very intensively on that. By that time, all the information was really -- I was cut off from all information in that respect at that time. Also I was not duty bound to know about that through official clan else. I dealt with counter-intelligence and other matters within the 5th Air Force Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand but now I see that you're looking at your duties quite formally. In the beginning, though, I read out Article 1 of the rules of service of the security services, what the basic tasks of the security organs are.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that rule, and I acted in accordance with that rule but in later articles of the same rules of service, it is stated that a member of the security service of the JNA does not act in relation to civilian structures, and so these detachments were then in a way working against the regulations in the rules of service but they received instructions for that in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did they have any sources in the civilian sector?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you have such sources?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not. What kind of a service would it be, and what kind of an organised state would it be, which -- in which the services would each have sources in one another?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about civilians as physical persons, and I'm not thinking about the civilian services as such. What I'm asking you is that were civilians as such sources for the security organs?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no because the security services were obliged to work along a network. It's a certain thing was of interest in relation to a civilian structure, with persons who were outside of the JNA, then this was a matter that was dealt with by the civilian security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, your unit, was -- did it need a replenishment of men, reinforcements, because members of the reserve force had been transferred to the police force and the figure mentioned is between 20.000 and 30.000 men in a very short period of time?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What unit of mine are you thinking about, the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it didn't have any problems with manpower. We received relatively small numbers from civilian structures and that is a well-known fact. The air force is replenished, 80 per cent of it was replenished with the men it had from its own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you answered questions linked to Mr. Bogdan Vujic and I don't want to ask you any more about that except to ask you whether the name Slavko Tomic means anything to you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did know some people with the surname Tomic from the service but I can't remember whether I actually knew Slavko Tomic. If you could tell me a little more about him perhaps that would ring a bell but there were several Tomics in the security service and the air force. There were men with the name of Tomic in the 5th army security department. There was a Tomic there. What his first name was, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Bogoljub Kijanovic? Does that seem familiar?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that there were a couple of questions, and through the transcript in Milosevic trial you answered several questions about the Keljmendi case, I think, and your answers are part of the exhibits. I'm just going to ask you whether you know that at that period, after the Keljmendi case, there were three similar cases of different barracks on the territory of Yugoslavia with the killing of soldiers, Albanian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about any killings but I do know from information that warnings were issued that that danger did exist, and that that possibility was a real possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also in the Milosevic trial, I'm not going to ask you about this, but you were asked about the national, the ethnic structure of the leading personages in the security service. You claimed that there were people of all ethnicities and that Vasiljevic, the deputy, was a Macedonian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to move on and ask you something about your career before and after these events. To the best of my knowledge, after the school of national defence that you attended, you were appointed president of the division committee of the SK on the air force and air defence system, is that true?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. I was just a member of the committee, the League of Communists committee in the SK and RVO, that is to say the air force. But before that while I was doing my duty in Bihac and for a time the provisional president and secretary of the committee, when the politician was reassigned somewhere, for a few months, as a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of your career then, does that mean that you held no party political functions? Is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I was a member of the committee of the League of Communists' committee. That's a high party function in the PVO and -- air defence and a secretary of the 117th fighter platoon. Now I was -- whether I was secretary of the basic organisation of the League of Communists, I don't know, but as a rule the security organs were not appointed and elected to committees. Well, some of them were but not to the top echelons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. That wasn't my question. I wasn't interested in that. I was interested in whether you, at the time, and you said you were a member of the committee, and that that was indeed a political appointment, a political post, whether you agree with me that one of the basic principles, fundamental principles of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, was brotherhood and unity, the principle of brotherhood an unity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was at the foundations of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. Well, what do you consider that principle of brotherhood and unity is? What was your position? In a sentence, explain to the Trial Chamber what that postulate means that was used so much in the former Yugoslavia, this concept of brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant a state of equal nations and nationalities as they were called within the frameworks of one and the same state. Enjoying equal rights, equal responsibilities and duties, and that means that nobody, that is to say no single nationality or ethnic group could be jeopardised and threatened due to their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that one -- that was one of the basic premises of the constitution, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the postulates of the constitution itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell on constitutional questions and historical issues. We'll hear testimony about that from other witnesses in due course. But I'm going to make an observation and you will tell me if I'm wrong. Yesterday during the -- your testimony and on Friday during your CV we see yourself and you see yourself first of all as a soldier. You wanted to stress that professional function of yours. And on the other hand, most of your career on the basis of most of your career I see that as a soldier you were always next to political structures, very much involved. Am I wrong in thinking that, in getting that impression?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No you're not wrong because a good soldier must think politically as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, you took the oath, the JNA oath, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Part of your career, your military career, was following one policy in politics and another portion was the opposite, a completely different policy and politics. One was communist and one, if I can put it in the following terms, was anti-communist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. My present political orientation, and involvement, for this kind of policy was a continuation of the beliefs I held earlier on, about equality, a democratic setup for states and a civilised behaviour and conduct for states and individuals, and that's what I endeavoured to achieve then and succeeded and that's what I'm doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm most interested in that transitional period, that is to say once you left the JNA and when you joined the Croatian political option, not joined in the sense -- well, we heard that you were not a member but you became close to the ruling oligarchy of the day in Croatia. Now, am I wrong in claiming that the HDZ as the ruling party was anticommunist?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then and now too. You're not wrong. That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in already back in 1990, in your office, you had prominently displayed the books, the works, of Franjo Tudjman, the dictionary of the new Croatian language, and Tudjman's other book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just testing the facts that I have been informed of.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have been informed wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll put that to you later during the Defence case. But to continue, on the basis of your biography, your CV, you asked permission to leave the second -- to leave the JNA on the 2nd of July 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you officially leave the JNA pursuant to that request, a short while afterwards or --

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the same day. At 7.30 I wrote my request, and at half past 1.00, I was told that I could go, was free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we received information as to when you took up your appointment as the Zenga chief but I'm interested in what you offered your services to the Croatian authorities. When was that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never offered my services. They called me to join up and I was very happy to do so after all the events that had taken place that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very soon you were appointed as chief of the Main Staff of the ZNG and very soon after that you became the principal negotiator on behalf of the Croatian government with the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we all agree that in view of the high security position that you occupied with the enemy, if I could put it that way, that you then had to be investigated by the people who had invited you to join up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody told me about any investigations, if they did check me out, then that's up to them. I accepted the invitation and started working straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about your security position, the one you held. A general question, just like the Prosecutor asked you. Is it logical to investigate somebody who was to be appointed to such a high position with the enemy? Is that logical?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether to investigate the individual or to have an opinion of him already formed. What was it in my case, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, am I wrong if I say that you during the previous period, that previous period, de facto had to prove yourself to your new employers? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't try to do anything like that. I always acted in accordance with my view of the world and my principles, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I be -- ask the Court for a pause now, a break? I don't have too many questions but I would like to stick to the timetable and continue with my questioning in this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Agha, might I inquire whether you would expect to be long in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No longer than 30 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at ten minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agotic, well, we are drawing to the end but I just have a few more questions and please just give me as short answers as possible, yes or no preferably, to give the Prosecution time to complete its re-examination. I asked you whether you took the oath of office when you joined the JNA, the solemn declaration, you said you had done that. Is it true that you, just like all the other security organs, when you joined up with the security service, that you signed a written statement binding -- with a confidentiality clause which was binding upon you, that you would keep the services secrets, that that was one of the principles? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember having signed anything but, yes, realistically speaking that would be realistic to suppose that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I wrong in saying that you have gone back fundamentally on both those things?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of that is correct. I claim that they parted ways with me, not with me trampling on them and parting ways with them, because that's where I was where I spent my whole life until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it correct that on the 31st of July 1991, in the Yugoslav People's Army, in Yugoslavia, you were decorated with the brotherhood and unity decoration?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My information tells me that it was July 1991; is that right? And I was a little taken aback when I saw that.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to see that because quite obviously that is something after my departure but I don't believe that is so. That's the first time that I have heard about this. But I would be happy if that were the case, if I were indeed decorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me go on. So you don't know that you received a decoration?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was decorated a number of times up until that date. That is to say JNA decorations, but not that particular decoration on the 31st of July 1991. I hear that for the first time. So please let them know that they can send it to me at my address.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, my information is that that led to a great revulsion amongst your colleagues because you had already left the JNA. So that's why I had to ask you that question, that there it was an uproar on the part of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. 31st of July, you say? Well, I left on the 2nd. I don't know. Perhaps somebody took it in the right way, in the proper light.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You got the Banja Lucica, Zrinksi decorations. They were awarded to you by the Croatian leadership; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a number of decorations. I don't know which, because I don't attach too much importance to one or another decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were given the medal for the Operation Storm? I read that in your CV.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Medals were given for operations Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to raise a legal matter now, which is linked to the following questions. That is to say I have few questions which emanate exclusively from written exhibits which were admitted and are to be found in the transcript of the Milosevic trial, that were admitted and introduced by the Defence. Those documents we received yesterday pursuant to Rule 68 from the Prosecution, when we read the transcripts we saw that Mr. Milosevic asked a certain number of questions and put forward or tendered three documents and those documents were admitted into evidence as part of the exhibits of that trial. Now, it is my opinion that those documents by way of the rules of service, should be an attachment to the transcript. So I consider that those exhibits should be admitted into evidence because, when you read about those exhibits and documents and you don't know what these refer to, you will not be able to weigh up his evidence without them. And they are documents which are linked to matters raised by Mr. Borovic for 1995, and once again it is my opinion that pursuant to Rule 90(H) -- have I got that number wrong? Yes, I think it is 90 (H), that when the witness is cross-examined with respect to credibility, cross-examination will be linked to the subject matter of the evidence in chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case, et cetera. I have three documents which I wish to admit into evidence and which were admitted into evidence in the Milosevic trial, and the transcript that was admitted here as an exhibit. And I have one question for each of these documents that I'd like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of what you told Mr. Borovic, that that is outside the frameworks of the examination, then I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Agha. You started off, Mr. Lukic, by saying that you were raising a matter. Did I understand you wanted answers again or were you simply putting on record your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the subject linked to the 1995 events, you told Mr. Borovic that they were matters that were outside the framework of the indictment, and the questions that I wish to ask emanate from the documents which were introduced into -- in that trial, admitted as evidence in that trial, related to those matters. I'm asking you whether I can tender those documents into evidence and, in relation to that, I'd like to ask him a few questions because they are linked to the transcript which is an exhibit in this -- these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate answers to one or two parts of what you have put, Mr. Lukic? First, the fact that the transcript of evidence in another trial is tendered doesn't bring with it any documents that became an exhibit in the course of that transcript. Hence, it was that Mr. Agha went through and specifically tendered exhibits that he thought were relevant to the evidence in this case, and I think judging from the cross-examination, Defence counsel have been in general agreement with Mr. Agha's selection of those documents. The decision has been given that the events of an entirely separate operation some years later, in 1995, have no direct bearing upon the facts of this case and appear to the Chamber to have so -- no sufficient weight on the issue of credibility to justify their exploration in this trial. Now, from what I understand you to say, the exhibits that you're interested in, from the Milosevic trial, relate to those events in 1995 and not to events in 1991. If that's the case, were you to move to tender them, on that basis alone, I would expect that the Chamber would not receive them. However, the Chamber has not seen these documents, has no idea whether there might be some other relevance or not. So you keep that in mind. If you think there is some particular relevance in one of those documents or more of them, we don't want to cut you off altogether, but if it is simply dealing with the events of 1995, our earlier ruling will prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. In that case, I would just like to show the witness one document, the document was given to us by the Prosecution yesterday so we didn't have time to scan it. I have prepared copies for the Chamber and for the witness, also for the Prosecution. The document dates from 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Agha was wanting to say something. I may have dealt with the matters that were in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, you have dealt with those matters which were in my mind and we can address this document separately on its merits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the witness is familiar with the document because, in the Milosevic case, when the witness testified, the document was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agotic, I'm going to ask you the following. Well, my colleague, Mr. Borovic, already asked you: My question will be the following: Are you familiar with this, let me put it that way, incident in relation to Busovaca? Your name is mentioned in the document. I'm interested if you have any information that during the war in Bosnia, Croatia assisted in any way in the logistics sense and you, also, in view of the job that you were performing were assisting the forces of the HVO. Do you know about this incident or this event in Busovaca and this HVO helicopter? Before you begin, I would like to clarify for the Trial Chamber where Divulje is. This is mentioned at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Divulje is in Split -- is near Split in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, would you please tell us what you know about this event, what happened? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did we assist logistically the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, specifically the HVO? Yes. We did. Both the HVO and the B and H army. We did help them by evacuating the wounded, supplying medical equipment, material, food, and, like I said, there were over 100 transporter flights by helicopter to this end. There were also a number of flights except for one time in June 1992 when there was an accident. This was a combat flight. And a comrade of mine or a companion of mine was killed in that action. He was downed somewhere in the area of Derventa that in an artillery operation where the Croatian side was being shelled. That is when a pilot was downed with his plane. There were no other combat flights other than that one. But there were these other logistical flights that I described. There were more than 100 of them. In this particular area, around Kiseljak, there were a lot of wounded and they were evacuated. The procedure was as following. The HVO or the B and H army, when they were in combat, would request such assistance and the procedure was that I, with the approval of my superiors, would approve such flights with this -- this condition that it had to be announced 48 hours before. What is mentioned here, this crew Katovic, Brkic, and this other person, they actually carried out a series of flights, Sejo Hodzic, they carried out a series of flights above Bosnia, the ones that I described. But it was all done with the approval of the Croatian side. However, no material was supplied that was of a combat nature or ammunition. That was not supplied with the official permission of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this information, it can be concluded that in this flight, 190.000 762-millimetre ammunition was distributed to Tomislavgrad, and that the European Community, actually the observers of who approve such things it were informed that allegedly the ill or the sick were being transported. Since they didn't know and didn't have time, it was alleged that these sick persons were in a coma and that there was not enough time to check. But anyway, maybe I can provide this document for you and you can read it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours the Prosecution would submit that not only is the line of questioning being adopted by the learned Defence counsel but also the document itself lacking in relevance to the particular charges in the indictment, namely that it's dated in 1993 and refers to the theatre of operations in Bosnia, not even in Croatia. So we would object to that on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained why I wanted to ask this question. According to me, this question refers to Rule 90(H) and it is my right to cross-examine about matters that have a bearing on the veracity of the witness, and in that sense, the credibility of the witness. So I'm not in that case in any way limited by the indictment. So in that sense, I believe that the document from 1993, in which the name of this witness is mentioned, and some other relevant facts are mentioned in respect of his knowledge, can be relevant in the establishing of the credibility of this witness. Facts were established in many cases from the present, if they have any kind of bearing on the credibility of the witness, and they don't necessarily have to be relevant to the actual indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what is the point about credibility that you make?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to state the fact derived from this document that, at that time, he was very informed about the purpose to which the so-called humanitarian flights were used in 1993, because that can be concluded on the basis of a sentence from this document from 1993. In that sense, I want to touch upon his credibility as a military person who discussed about his knowledge of events in the period from the indictment concerning the Vukovar events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have difficulty following that, Mr. Lukic, frankly. Are you saying that this flight in 1993 was typical of flights in 1991, and that it shows that the evidence given by this witness about events in 1991 therefore is not reliable, or what? Or are you saying simply, well, this was a flight that was conducted in some dishonest way in 1993; therefore, the evidence of this witness about everything in 1991 should come under suspicion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying, Your Honours, that it can be concluded on the basis of this document that HVO forces in Herceg-Bosna, not in Croatia but in Herceg-Bosna, enjoyed logistical support from Croatia in 1993 and used information in respect of the European monitoring commission by deceiving them as regarding the use of humanitarian convoys. We talked about the convoy from October today and he expressed his clear position on why humanitarian convoys were used, and I wanted to actually compromise the testimony of the witness in that respect based on this document. These are my arguments, exclusively relating to that part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you want to put to the witness that in 1991, convoys or a convoy - I think we've heard only of two - for humanitarian reasons were used for some military purposes instead? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that there could be suspicions on the part of the JNA that a convoy or a part of the convoy or a vehicle or a person were being used counter to the purposes of the convoy itself. That is my main assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view, Mr. Lukic, that we see no sufficient relevance. What occurred in 1993, some significant period of time later, in respect of a different theatre would provide no foundation for the JNA to have suspicions or views in 1991 in respect of what was occurring in Vukovar. So the ruling is not demonstrated relevance to credit or to the facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case, I have completed my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Agha?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to touch upon various points arising from your cross-examination which hopefully you can deal with and clarify for us. Now, the first topic I want to look at is that of security officers and their organs on which you were cross-examined. Now, during cross-examination, you stated in your evidence that a security officer was not authorised to hand over a civilian suspected of committing a crime in relation to the JNA and that they could detain that person with the investigative organs, until those investigative organs arrived. Now, are you familiar with the rules of service for the security organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1984?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the rules of service, and this was not provided under the rules. Or actually it was provided for under the rules, but in the way that I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the leave of the court and the assistance of the Court clerk, I'd like to call up a document for the general to view and this is 65 ter 394, bearing B/C/S ERN 00909817 and English ERN 00920099.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when this document appears, General, it is actually the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces of the SFRY 1984, and -- do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can I kindly ask the Court clerk to take us to page 19 and paragraph 46? Now, General, do you have a copy of paragraph 46?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have pages 36 and 37 and not the pages that we need. We need to see paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: It's page 19 in the English, if that's of assistance. Page 19.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can go by the actual paragraph, so it would be paragraph 46 or item 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Item 46.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, it says "authorised officers of security organs have the right to use physical force for the purposes of overcoming resistance by a person who is taken into custody or," and this is the important part for us, "or for the purposes of repelling an attack against themselves or a person for whom they are providing security. In carrying out within their competence authorised officers of security organs may use," and again importantly, "firearms only if they have no other way of protecting people's lives." Now, would your interpretation of that rule be that a security organ is obliged to also protect the people whom it is detaining?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If being given such an assignment, then yes, because the rules of service do provide for that. It doesn't say which people, but it does say the lives of people. So that can also refer to prisoners, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And in so doing it specifically provides that the security officers can resort to force, if need be?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's how it's regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I ask the Chamber that this document be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 107, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, as a senior military officer, what would you define the capabilities of the Guards Brigade as, in terms of their ability to protect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask whether this exceeds the ambit of the cross-examination because none of the defence teams asked any questions about the capabilities of the Guards Brigade. Throughout the whole time, in view of his position, the witness did provide answers which were more than just the answers of a factual witness, but were answers more suitable to be covered by an expert witness. We do intend to bring expert witnesses on these topics. But also throughout the cross-examinations, there were no questions posed regarding the capabilities of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: As indicated earlier in cross-examination, the question arose as the ability to detain and the regulation which has just been exhibited also refers to the ability to protect. The obligation, indeed, to protect. So my question stems from whether the Guards Brigade or the security organ within it had the ability to protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Protect what?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Protect persons whom it was detaining or who it had under its control, was providing security from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't see this as arising, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I move now, General, to a second matter which arose out of your cross-examination and that is in respect of Mr. Bogdan Vujic. Now, in your cross-examination, you referred to a security officer named Colonel Bogdan Vujic whom you had contact with. In your evidence, one of his tasks was to identify irredentist threesomes, so would it follow that Colonel Vujic had an expertise in identifying specified individuals from within a particular group?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Colonel Vujic worked on the implementation of Albanian nationalism and irredentism in the ranks of the JNA and he had a lot of experience in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So if, say, the JNA wanted to determine whether there was any combatants within a group of civilians, would that be an area in which Colonel Vujic would have expertise and the ability to deal with?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vujic had many years of experience and both in his professional capacity and in life experience, he was familiar with the situation in the army and in the civilian structures because he had a lot of contact with civilians in the course of his work, while dealing with the cases that I spoke about. How he dealt with the problem now, during this last war, I don't know. However, I had a very solid opinion of him based on what I knew and on my meetings with him at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you've already mentioned in cross-examination that you regarded him as an honourable officer. Did you also regard him as a professional officer who would carry out his duties according to the law?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I considered him to be a good, professional soldier. A professional takes arguments into account, and I think that he did take arguments into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to come now to a different area which was addressed in your cross-examination, and this concerns the Vukovar defenders. Now, roughly, in October and November 1991, how many Vukovar defenders were there? A rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, never more than 1.500, 600, up to 1.700 within Vukovar, within the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And within that time frame, roughly how many or what was the strength of the JNA forces which they were facing?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say with any precision but I do know that from Vojvodina, the Dadik [phoen] Brigade was brought in, which, if it was in full strength had four and a half, maybe 5.000 men. That's how many men the brigades of the JNA numbered. On the other hand, units were brought in from the Novi Sad corps, and there were several units, what strength and rank they were is difficult for me to say but I do know that the units of the Novi Sad Corps took up the area of Baranja, north of the Drava river. They took control of the area to the south of the Drava River, east of Osijek, towards Erdut, Dalj, Sarvas, Aljmas, and the villages which spread towards Vukovar and the southeast. So most probably, in my estimate, it would be about 15.000 JNA soldiers who were engaged in the north and more southerly, the Guards Brigade, and the corps unit. Now, how many artillery units there were on the other side of the Danube, which assisted and reinforced them, in addition to the air force from the Batajnica airport and the air force from the Tuzla airport, is difficult for me to say, to give you any figures. But it was significant support both in artillery terms and in air force terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how would you compare the fire power which the Vukovar defenders had with that of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incomparable because the defenders of Vukovar had mortars, that was the strongest type of weapon, whether it was a 120-millimetre mortar, I'm not quite sure. They had no artillery. They had firearms. And on the JNA side, there was the Guards Brigade unit, which was well armed and well capacitated and trained because it numbered the best soldiers that the JNA had, the best-trained men. So that any ratio would be unrealistic. They couldn't be compared. The ratio of forces couldn't be compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: But what about the armour, in terms of artillery, tanks and this kind of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I number that amongst the overall JNA forces, and I know for sure very reliable information from a foreign military representative, military envoy, who told me in 1992 or 1993 perhaps, that he had monitored this, it was a British colonel, air force colonel, and that he monitored the fire from the left banks of the river in the battle of Vukovar, and that on the other side, there was no counteraction because it is only the artillery that can be deployed to neutralise this. As regards the armoured weapons, I can't say how many numbers but the general public heard about large numbers of tanks destroyed, large numbers of tanks deployed, but I never delved into an estimation of how much of what there was. And the JNA will be best placed to tell you about that. But I do know, Mr. Prosecutor, that Vukovar was targeted with planes of the highest calibre, a bomb fell on the hospital itself. It was a 250 kilogram bomb which was the largest bomb that the JNA had amongst its arsenal of weapons which did not explode, and that is proof positive that the hospital was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, turning to another area of your cross-examination, you were asked numerous questions about various JNA barracks located in Croatia. Now, with regard to the Vukovar barracks, roughly on what date was this deblocked by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that barracks was never blocked because it was stationed on that kind of terrain, that is to say the southeastern reaches of Vukovar, that general location, and it had an open space in front of it towards villages which were predominantly inhabited by a Serb population, which was well-disposed towards JNA units. They even supported them. And so those barracks was never in a classical blockade as were the other barracks on the territory of the Republic of Croatia which were under the control of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So even when the barracks was in JNA control, was there still shelling of Vukovar or was there not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an automatic indicator that when the first convoy arrived for the evacuation of the casualties in the barracks, it was under the control of the JNA, and it was only then that the strongest shelling started, which led up to the fall of Vukovar. So there is no dilemma there whatsoever. My answer is positive, the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Can you deduce from that that the mission of the JNA in Eastern Slavonia was beyond the deblocking of the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The JNA did have that assignment. Deep penetration with its elite units into the depth of the Republic of Croatia with the aim of achieving the variant that I termed variant A and then later on after the plan was corrected it was plan B. They resorted to plan B, and having encountered resistance from the Croatian side they remained in the area nor a long time, there was pressure from the international community, and then they agreed to plan C, which implied for these particular unit which attacked Vukovar and the Eastern Slavonia the realisation of the plan to take control of the eastern part which was later called Sector East, upon the arrival of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, another area I'd like to move to is that of the first evacuation which came up numerous times in cross-examination. Now, you mention in your evidence that there was a successful first evacuation in October, when Medecins Sans Frontieres accompanied the convoy to and from the hospital in Vukovar with its patients. Now, what was the fate of those patients on that convoy which was accompanied by Medecins Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those casualties, most of them were seriously wounded persons with amputated limbs, I think about 110, 112, I can't guarantee the number, but they were, after a lot of trouble and several days, taken to hospitals on the Croatian side and were put up, most of them, in the hospital at Nasice and the rest were transported to the hospitals in Zagreb. Some of those individuals from the first convoy I know myself personally, and some of them survived, others succumbed and died immediately after the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, on the questions of evacuations, it would seem that the next evacuation was on 20th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my -- the Prosecutor to remind me who of the Defence team mentioned the evacuation of the 20th of November and then I'll give up my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that during the various cross-examinations of the learned Defence counsel there was some confusion as to how many evacuations there actually were and when they took place, so the purpose of the question is to clarify that there were in fact two evacuations, one which is in October, which we've just discussed, and that there was only one more second one, which was the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That may be pursued, Mr. Lukic. But you're on notice, Mr. Agha, you can't go much beyond that without satisfying the Chamber about Mr. Lukic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So, General, moving now to the second evacuation, which was on the 20th November 1991, based on the evacuation agreement which you've already discussed in your evidence. Now, this evacuation went without the Red Cross, without the Medecins Sans Frontieres or ECMM monitors and had a JNA escort with about 300 patients, what was the fate of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, you've immediately gone beyond whether there were two evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've won, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So, Witness, we'll move away from the second or however many evacuations there were and come to a different area of your cross-examination. And this concerned the director of the hospital. Now, during cross-examination, you mentioned that the director of the hospital was in close contact with the commissioner of Vukovar. Who was the director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was Dr. Vesna Bosanac, a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: You also mentioned during your cross-examination that the hospital had special needs such as supplies to be protected. How often, if at all, were you contacted regarding the needs of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vesna Bosanac, precisely, from the hospital. I didn't contact anybody else, nor did anybody else contact me, because from the 8th of October, when I was with her for the first time onwards, sometimes during the day she would call me up two or three times. At other times, she wouldn't call for several days but would contact the chief of the Main Staff, the Minister of Health, because they informed me about that, and every time emphasising the grievous problems she had with the large number of casualties, not having enough medical supplies, the fact that the hospital was fired at, was shelled. So that I was very often on the phone with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned in your cross-examination that you had reports from Dedakovic and Borkovic, sometimes on a daily basis, during the siege of Vukovar, requesting for equipment, manpower and so forth. Did they ever report to you about the shelling of Vukovar and about the hospital and its requirements and needs?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't say specifically send me such and such, because they knew that I wasn't able to do that. But they did inform me about the difficult situation and about the shelling of the hospital, and even their assessments. It was difficult to count but I would hear of their assessments that during the course of one day in Vukovar, as many as 5.000 projectiles fell on the town, artillery ones, mortar ones, et cetera, with a large number of projectiles targeting the hospital and hitting the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, finally I'd like to come to the topic of the so-called arming of Croatia and the Spegelj affair which has been delved into during cross-examination. Now, you've mentioned to the Chamber that -- and I think the Chamber has accepted that you have the ability to answer questions with a political flavour as well as military. So I want to ask you, under the SFRY constitution, the SFRY was obliged to provide weapons to each republic for the police and the TO. Now, in 1990-1991, how many weapons was the SFRY providing Croatia for its police and TO, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SSNO didn't provide the police with weapons, and the Territorial Defence. It gave permission and authorisation that -- for production in factories of the former Yugoslav republics, that weapons could be procured if they were paid for and based on a plan, to arm the Territorial Defence, each republic set aside 0.5 per cent of its GDP for procuring resources and maintenance of resources and training as well, and from the point when in mid-May 1990 there was an order by the head of the General Staff decreeing that weapons be confiscated, of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, not a single bullet, not a single weapon, was issued by the SSNO, was given to the Republic of Croatia after 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now under the SFRY constitution, if the federal government was failing to provide arms to a republic, which it was entitled to, for example, the police, or TO, what if any right did the republic have to acquire weapons themselves?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the republic had any right based on some written law and regulation to acquire weapons from other sources. That is to say from abroad. However, the development of the political situation was such that the chances of having the federal secretary return Croatian weapons to Croatia, or to turn the tap on for procurement from the warehouses of the former Yugoslavia, were equal to zero. Therefore, if Croatia thought that it would be jeopardised, it had to arm itself, and that is how it solved the problem. It solved the problem in the way it did. I did not take part in that but we can see the way in which this was resolved later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: What about the police force of a republic? Whose responsibility is it to arm the police force?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To arm the police force was, in the former Yugoslavia, a unified process and this was done by the Ministry of the Interior of the republic, and it was in charge of supplying and equipping its military police units. It was not only from domestic sources but procurement from abroad as well. However, for as long as Yugoslavia functioned as a united whole, I do believe that that was done with the knowledge of the ministry, the federal Ministry of the Interior, the Yugoslav Internal Affairs Ministry. Now, whether that was like that afterwards and when that was -- principle was upset, I think it was probably after the elections in 1990 when there was greater distrust among -- between the federal and republican organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, General, that completes the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Agha. There was one question of Mr. Agha's, General, to which the answer is unclear. You said that after the order for confiscation of weapons in May of 1990, there was not a single weapon or bullet issued to the Republic of Croatia. Was that -- you went on then to add words, after 1990 and 1991. And they are the words that confuse the Chamber. Are you saying that there were no weapons and bullets issued after the end of the period 1990-1991, or are you saying there were none issued after the confiscation order in 1990? Could you help to clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know when the last weapon or branches of the Ministry of the Interior or Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia weapons as consignments reached Croatia in an organised fashion, and with the knowledge of the federal secretary for National Defence and the chief of the General Staff, and I have in mind here the period of up to the 15th of May 1990. However, when on the 15th of May 1990, the chief of the General Staff issued orders that all weapons of the Territorial Defence of Croatia be placed under the control of the JNA, from that moment on, not a single lethal weapon or explosive or device reached the Republic of Croatia through regular channels, the regular channels of supply through the federal secretary or the other usual ways from the factories and production line that existed in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies that question. Now, General, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions and your evidence. The Chamber is grateful for your attendance and your assistance, and you are now able to return to your ordinary activities. Thank you very much, indeed. Given the hour, clearly we will adjourn now rather than call a fresh witness. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
